blocks.body:
The prime number theorem says that $\psi(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n)$ is asymptotic to $x$, equivalently that $\pi(x)\sim\operatorname{li}(x)$. It says nothing about how large the error is. Riemann's 1859 paper showed where the error comes from: each nontrivial zero $\rho$ of the zeta function contributes a wave of size about $x^{\operatorname{Re}\rho}$ to $\psi(x)-x$. The Riemann hypothesis is the statement that all these waves have the smallest possible size, $\sqrt x$.

Riemann wrote that it was "very likely" that all nontrivial zeros have real part $\tfrac12$, and set the question aside. It became part of Hilbert's eighth problem in 1900 and one of the Clay Millennium Problems in 2000. It is open as of October 2026. This lesson states it precisely, proves the easy half of its equivalence with the error term in the prime number theorem, surveys what is known, and explains why it is hard.

blocks.title: The zeros of zeta
blocks.body:
Recall from [[zeta]] and [[functional-equation]]: for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$,

$$\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}=\prod_p\big(1-p^{-s}\big)^{-1},$$

and $\zeta$ continues to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb C$ whose only pole is a simple pole at $s=1$. The Euler product shows $\zeta(s)\ne0$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$. The functional equation relates $s$ and $1-s$; it produces the trivial zeros $-2,-4,-6,\dots$ and shows that all other zeros, the nontrivial zeros $\rho=\beta+i\gamma$, lie in the critical strip $0\le\beta\le1$. Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin proved (1896) that there are none on the line $\beta=1$, which is the analytic heart of the [[pnt|prime number theorem]]; so in fact $0< \beta<1$.

The nontrivial zeros come in symmetric families: if $\rho$ is a zero, so are $\bar\rho$ (because $\zeta(\bar s)=\overline{\zeta(s)}$) and $1-\rho$ (by the functional equation). As shown in [[nontrivial-zeros]], the number of zeros with $0< \gamma\le T$ is

$$N(T)=\frac T{2\pi}\log\frac T{2\pi}-\frac T{2\pi}+\frac78+O(\log T),$$

so there are infinitely many, with average spacing about $2\pi/\log(T/2\pi)$ at height $T$. The first one is $\tfrac12+14.1347\ldots i$.

blocks.title: The Riemann hypothesis (conjecture)
blocks.body:
Every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function lies on the critical line:

$$\zeta(\rho)=0,\ 0< \operatorname{Re}\rho<1\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{Re}\rho=\tfrac12.$$

This is a conjecture, not a theorem. It is open as of October 2026.

blocks.title: Why zeros control primes
blocks.body:
The link with primes is the [[explicit-formula]]: for $x>1$ not a prime power,

$$\psi(x)=x-\sum_\rho\frac{x^\rho}{\rho}-\log2\pi-\tfrac12\log\big(1-x^{-2}\big),$$

where the sum runs over nontrivial zeros, taken symmetrically ($|\gamma|< T$, then $T\to\infty$). A zero $\rho=\beta+i\gamma$ and its conjugate together contribute $-2\operatorname{Re}(x^\rho/\rho)$, an oscillation in $\log x$ with frequency $\gamma$ and amplitude $2x^\beta/|\rho|$. So the size of $\psi(x)-x$ is governed by

$$\Theta=\sup\{\operatorname{Re}\rho:\ \zeta(\rho)=0,\ 0< \operatorname{Re}\rho<1\}.$$

By the symmetry $\rho\mapsto1-\rho$ and the existence of zeros on the line, $\tfrac12\le\Theta\le1$, and the Riemann hypothesis is exactly the statement $\Theta=\tfrac12$. Making the heuristic precise requires a truncated form of the explicit formula with an error term, and leads to the following.

blocks.title: RH and the error term
blocks.body:
1. If $\psi(x)=x+O(x^\alpha)$ for some $\alpha<1$, then $\zeta(s)\ne0$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>\alpha$.
2. (von Koch, 1901) If the Riemann hypothesis holds, then $\psi(x)=x+O(\sqrt x\log^2x)$, and equivalently $\pi(x)=\operatorname{li}(x)+O(\sqrt x\log x)$.

Consequently the Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to: $\psi(x)=x+O(x^{1/2+\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

blocks.title: Proof of part 1 and of the equivalence
blocks.body:
We prove part 1; part 2 needs the truncated explicit formula and is omitted (see Davenport or Titchmarsh).

For $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, $-\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s)=\sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-s}$. Partial summation (see [[partial-summation]]) gives $$\sum_{n\le N}\Lambda(n)n^{-s}=\psi(N)N^{-s}+s\int_1^N\psi(x)x^{-s-1}\,dx$$, and $\psi(N)N^{-s}\to0$ because $\psi(N)\le N\log N$. Hence

$$-\frac{\zeta'(s)}{\zeta(s)}=s\int_1^\infty\psi(x)\,x^{-s-1}\,dx\qquad(\operatorname{Re}s>1).$$

Write $\psi(x)=x+E(x)$ with $|E(x)|\le Cx^\alpha$ for $x\ge1$. Since $s\int_1^\infty x\cdot x^{-s-1}\,dx=\frac s{s-1}$,

$$-\frac{\zeta'(s)}{\zeta(s)}=\frac s{s-1}+s\int_1^\infty E(x)\,x^{-s-1}\,dx.$$

The integrand is bounded by $Cx^{\alpha-\sigma-1}$ with $\sigma=\operatorname{Re}s$, so the integral converges absolutely and locally uniformly in $\operatorname{Re}s>\alpha$ and defines a holomorphic function there. So the right side is holomorphic in $\operatorname{Re}s>\alpha$ except for the pole at $s=1$. The left side is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$, and the two sides agree on $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, so by the identity theorem they agree on $\operatorname{Re}s>\alpha$. But at a zero $\rho$ of $\zeta$ of multiplicity $m\ge1$, the function $-\zeta'/\zeta$ has a pole with residue $-m$. Hence $\zeta$ has no zeros with $\operatorname{Re}s>\alpha$.

For the equivalence: if $\psi(x)=x+O(x^{1/2+\varepsilon})$ for all $\varepsilon>0$, part 1 rules out zeros with real part above $\tfrac12$, and the symmetry $\rho\mapsto1-\rho$ rules out zeros with real part below $\tfrac12$. The converse is part 2.

blocks.title: Best possible, and equivalent forms
blocks.body:
The exponent $\tfrac12$ cannot be lowered: Littlewood proved in 1914 that $\psi(x)-x$ takes values larger than $c\sqrt x\log\log\log x$ and smaller than $-c\sqrt x\log\log\log x$ for arbitrarily large $x$, and that $\pi(x)-\operatorname{li}(x)$ changes sign infinitely often. So RH says the error term in the prime number theorem is as small as it could possibly be, up to logarithms. Assuming RH, Schoenfeld (1976) made this explicit: $|\pi(x)-\operatorname{li}(x)|< \frac1{8\pi}\sqrt x\log x$ for $x\ge2657$.

There are many other equivalent forms. Two elementary ones:

- (Littlewood) RH holds if and only if the Mertens function $M(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\mu(n)$ satisfies $M(x)=O(x^{1/2+\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon>0$ (see [[mobius]]).
- (Robin, 1984) RH holds if and only if $\sigma(n)< e^\gamma\,n\log\log n$ for every $n>5040$, where $\sigma$ is the sum of divisors (see [[arithmetic-functions]]) and $\gamma$ is Euler's constant.

blocks.title: What is known
blocks.body:
Zeros on the line. Hardy proved in 1914 that infinitely many zeros have real part $\tfrac12$. Hardy and Littlewood (1921) showed that the number of such zeros up to height $T$ is at least $cT$; Selberg (1942) improved this to a positive proportion of all zeros; Levinson (1974) reached more than one third, and Conrey (1989) more than two fifths.

Zeros away from the line. Unconditionally one knows only a [[zero-free-region]] of the form $\beta>1-c/\log|\gamma|$ (de la Vallée Poussin), later widened by Vinogradov and Korobov, which still shrinks towards the line $\operatorname{Re}s=1$ as $|\gamma|\to\infty$. Nobody can rule out zeros with real part $0.999$ at great height. Even the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, that $\Theta<1$, has resisted classical methods; see [[quasi-rh]] for its status. What is known is that zeros off the line must be rare: [[zero-density]] estimates bound how many zeros can have real part above $\sigma>\tfrac12$.

Computation. Riemann himself computed the first few zeros; his method, recovered from his notes by Siegel in 1932, became the Riemann–Siegel formula. Modern computations have checked that all zeros with $0< \gamma\le3\cdot10^{12}$ are on the line (Platt and Trudgian, 2021); by the formula for $N(T)$ that is more than $10^{13}$ zeros.

blocks.title: Why it is hard
blocks.body:
Several features make RH resistant.

- No known mechanism. The methods that give zero-free regions estimate $\zeta$ near $\operatorname{Re}s=1$ using the Euler product and exponential sums. Their output weakens as $|t|$ grows and does not come close to the line $\tfrac12$.
- The Euler product is essential. Davenport and Heilbronn (1936) found Dirichlet series with a functional equation of the same kind as $\zeta$ but no Euler product, and with zeros off the line. Any proof must use multiplicativity in an essential way.
- Computation cannot decide it. Numerical evidence is overwhelming, but number theory has phenomena that appear only at enormous heights; $\pi(x)< \operatorname{li}(x)$ holds for every $x$ ever computed and yet fails infinitely often.

There are reasons for optimism. The analogue for curves over finite fields was proved by Weil in the 1940s, and the corresponding statement for all varieties over [[finite-fields]] by Deligne in 1974, in both cases using geometry (an action of Frobenius) that has no known counterpart for $\zeta$. The Hilbert–Pólya idea seeks a self-adjoint operator whose eigenvalues are the ordinates $\gamma$, which would force them to be real. Montgomery's 1973 [[pair-correlation]] conjecture and Odlyzko's computations show that the zeros are spaced like eigenvalues of large random Hermitian matrices, which supports this picture without supplying the operator. In another direction, Rodgers and Tao (2018) proved that the de Bruijn–Newman constant satisfies $\Lambda\ge0$; RH is equivalent to $\Lambda\le0$, so RH, if true, is only barely true in this sense.

blocks.title: What a proof would imply
Counting zeros
blocks.body: Count the zeros with $0< \gamma<100$ numerically and compare with the main terms of $N(T)$.
blocks.solution:
Computing zeros (for example with mpmath's zetazero) gives the first zero at $\tfrac12+14.1347i$, the $29$th at $\tfrac12+98.8312i$ and the $30$th at $\tfrac12+101.3179i$. So $N(100)=29$, and all $29$ have real part $\tfrac12$ to working precision.

The main terms give $\frac{100}{2\pi}\log\frac{100}{2\pi}-\frac{100}{2\pi}+\frac78\approx29.002$. The agreement is much better than the $O(\log T)$ error term guarantees; the error term $S(T)=\frac1\pi\arg\zeta(\tfrac12+iT)$ is small on average and grows only very slowly.

blocks.title: The error term in practice
blocks.body: Compare $\pi(x)$ with $\operatorname{li}(x)$ for $x=10^4,10^5,10^6,10^7$, and with Schoenfeld's conditional bound $\frac1{8\pi}\sqrt x\log x$.
blocks.solution:
With $\operatorname{li}(x)=\int_0^x\frac{dt}{\log t}$ (principal value):

- $x=10^4$: $\pi=1229$, $\operatorname{li}\approx1246.1$, difference $\approx17.1$; bound $\approx36.6$.
- $x=10^5$: $\pi=9592$, $\operatorname{li}\approx9629.8$, difference $\approx37.8$; bound $\approx144.9$.
- $x=10^6$: $\pi=78498$, $\operatorname{li}\approx78627.5$, difference $\approx129.5$; bound $\approx549.7$.
- $x=10^7$: $\pi=664579$, $\operatorname{li}\approx664918.4$, difference $\approx339.4$; bound $\approx2028.0$.

The difference grows roughly like $\sqrt x/\log x$, well inside the bound. Note that $\pi(x)< \operatorname{li}(x)$ in every row; by Littlewood this inequality nevertheless reverses for some enormous $x$.

blocks.title: Rebuilding primes from zeros
blocks.body: Use the explicit formula with the first $50$ pairs of zeros to approximate $\psi(20.5)$ and $\psi(50.5)$.
blocks.solution:
The exact values are $\psi(20.5)=\log(2^4\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19)\approx19.2657$ and $\psi(50.5)\approx49.4854$.

The truncated formula $x-2\sum_{k\le50}\operatorname{Re}\frac{x^{\rho_k}}{\rho_k}-\log2\pi-\frac12\log(1-x^{-2})$, with $\rho_k=\tfrac12+i\gamma_k$ the first $50$ zeros in the upper half-plane, gives about $19.280$ at $x=20.5$ and $49.667$ at $x=50.5$. A few dozen zeros already locate the jumps of $\psi$ at the prime powers. Each term has amplitude $2\sqrt x/|\rho_k|$; if some zero had real part $\beta>\tfrac12$, its term would grow like $x^\beta$ and eventually dominate.

blocks.title: Robin's inequality
blocks.body: Show that $n=5040$ violates Robin's inequality $\sigma(n)< e^\gamma n\log\log n$, and check the inequality for $5040< n\le10^5$.
blocks.solution:
$5040=2^4\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot7$, so $\sigma(5040)=31\cdot13\cdot6\cdot8=19344$. On the other side, $e^\gamma\approx1.78107$ and $\log\log5040\approx2.1430$, giving $e^\gamma\cdot5040\cdot\log\log5040\approx19237$. So $\sigma(5040)>e^\gamma\,5040\log\log5040$, which is why Robin's criterion starts after $5040$.

A direct computation confirms the inequality for all $5040< n\le10^5$, as RH predicts. If RH were false, Robin's theorem guarantees a counterexample $n>5040$, but it says nothing about how large it would be, so checking finitely many $n$ proves nothing about RH.

blocks.body:
- RH concerns the nontrivial zeros only; the trivial zeros $-2,-4,\dots$ are not on the critical line and do not contradict it.
- "Infinitely many zeros on the line" (Hardy) and "more than two fifths of the zeros on the line" (Conrey) are far from "all zeros on the line".
- The equivalence with the prime number theorem needs $x^{1/2+\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon$; an error $O(x^{0.6})$ would give only $\Theta\le0.6$.
- Verifying $10^{13}$ zeros is strong evidence but not proof, and there are classical examples of number-theoretic statements failing only at astronomical sizes.
- The functional equation alone does not force zeros onto the line (Davenport–Heilbronn); any purported proof that uses only it is wrong.

RH sits on top of [[nontrivial-zeros]] and the [[explicit-formula]]. Its natural extension to Dirichlet $L$-functions is the [[grh]], which controls primes in arithmetic progressions. Weaker unconditional substitutes are [[zero-free-region|zero-free regions]] and [[zero-density]] estimates, and a weaker conjecture is the [[quasi-rh|quasi-Riemann hypothesis]]. RH implies the [[lindelof|Lindelöf hypothesis]] and sharp bounds for gaps between primes ([[prime-patterns]]). The statistics of the zeros connect to random matrix theory through [[pair-correlation]], and the proven analogue over [[finite-fields]] is one of the high points of twentieth-century mathematics. Equivalent forms run through [[mobius|the Mertens function]] and [[arithmetic-functions|the divisor sum]].

1. Using the symmetries $\rho\mapsto\bar\rho$ and $\rho\mapsto1-\rho$, show that a zero off the critical line would come with three other zeros, and describe where they lie.
2. Explain why $\Theta\ge\tfrac12$ unconditionally.
3. Show that if $\psi(x)=x+O(x^{3/4})$ were proved, it would imply that $\zeta$ has no zeros with real part greater than $\tfrac34$, and say what it would imply for zeros with real part less than $\tfrac14$.
4. Compute the amplitude $2\sqrt x/|\rho_1|$ of the first zero's contribution to $\psi(x)-x$ at $x=10^6$, and compare it with the actual value of $\psi(10^6)-10^6$.
